m.how: Tap any stock in the watchlist. The chart, market depth and day stats switch to it.
m.c: Each row shows the last traded price (LTP) and the change since yesterday's close. Indices such as NIFTY 50 are benchmarks: you can watch them, but you can't buy them directly.

m.how: Read the market depth under the chart, then answer the question below.
m.c: Market depth lists the five best bids (buyers) and offers (sellers). The gap between the best bid and the best offer is the spread. You buy at the offer and sell at the bid, so every round trip starts a spread behind.

m.how: Start the trading day, open a stock, press Buy, choose Market and place the order.
m.c: A market order fills immediately against the best offers in the book. You get speed, not a guaranteed price: a large order walks up the book and pays more.

m.how: Close the position with Exit in the Positions tab, or place an opposite order for the same quantity.
m.c: Every executed order costs money: brokerage, STT, exchange transaction charges, the SEBI fee, stamp duty and GST. The Funds tab shows exactly what your round trip cost.

m.t: Get filled with a limit order
m.how: Place a LIMIT buy a little below the best offer (or a sell above the best bid) and wait for the market to come to you.
m.c: A limit order sets the worst price you will accept, and it may never fill. When the price only touches your limit you may still be waiting in the queue behind earlier orders at that price.

m.how: In the Orders tab, press Modify on an open order and change its price or quantity.
m.c: Pending orders block margin until they fill or are cancelled. Changing the price sends your order to the back of the queue at the new price.

m.how: While you hold a position, place an SL-M order on the opposite side with the trigger beyond your entry (below it for a long).
m.c: A stop-loss sleeps until the last traded price crosses its trigger. Then it becomes a market order (SL-M) or a limit order (SL). Decide where the trade is wrong before you enter it.

m.t: Let the stop do its job
m.how: Keep a stop in place until it triggers and closes the position.
m.c: Stops feel bad when they hit. They exist so one bad trade cannot erase ten good ones. An SL (limit) stop can be skipped in a fast fall; an SL-M will fill, but possibly at a worse price.

m.how: Place an order with the product set to Intraday (MIS).
m.c: MIS gives up to 5× leverage: only about 20% of the position value is blocked as margin. Profit and loss are on the full position, so a 2% move against you is 10% of the margin you put up.

m.how: With MIS selected, Sell first, then Buy back the same quantity to close.
m.c: Short selling profits from a fall. In the cash market you can only short intraday; open MIS positions are squared off automatically before the close.

m.how: Buy with the product set to Longterm (CNC) and end the day still holding it.
m.c: CNC (cash and carry) needs the full amount and has no leverage. Shares reach your demat as holdings after T+1 settlement. Delivery has zero brokerage at Zerodha, but STT is 0.1% on both the buy and the sell.

m.how: Take at least one MIS trade and close every MIS position yourself before 15:25.
m.c: At 15:25 the broker squares off open MIS positions and charges ₹50 + GST per order. Plan your exits before the bell.

m.how: In the order window, type a stop-loss price in the risk planner, press "Size for 1% risk", then place the order.
m.c: Position size = (capital × risk per trade) ÷ (entry − stop). Risking 1% a trade means a ten-trade losing streak costs about 10% of the account, not all of it.

m.how: Close a trade whose profit is at least twice the risk you planned in the risk planner.
m.c: R is the amount you planned to lose on a trade. Measuring results in R makes trades of different sizes comparable. With 2R winners you can be right only 40% of the time and still make money.

m.how: Finish a trading day with a net profit after all charges.
m.c: Gross profit is what the chart shows. Net profit is what reaches your bank. Many small trades can be profitable gross and losing net.

m.how: Finish a day with at least three completed trades and an intraday drawdown under 1% of capital.
m.c: Drawdown is the fall from the day's peak account value. Keeping it small keeps your decisions calm.

m.how: In the Journal tab, give five completed trades a setup tag.
m.c: Tagging setups (breakout, pullback, VWAP, reversal) shows which ideas actually make money. It is also the dataset you will feed to a backtest.

m.how: Buy as price moves back above VWAP after closing below it within the last five minutes (or short the reverse).
m.c: VWAP is the volume-weighted average price for the day, drawn as the gold line on the chart. Intraday traders and execution algorithms treat it as the day’s fair value.

m.how: Over your last ten completed trades, reach a profit factor of 1.2 or more, net of charges.
m.c: Profit factor = total won ÷ total lost. Above 1 the method makes money. Judge a method on many trades, never on one.

m.how: Export your trade log as a CSV file from the Journal tab.
m.c: The companion Python project reads this file, and it runs the same order logic as an automated strategy. That is the bridge from clicking buttons to algorithmic trading.
